name: Jinx — The Coin That Lands Sideways

pages.name: Quick Reference
pages.html:
Every tier of the Coin asks the same question in a louder voice: you have already succeeded, so are you going to push it again? The item is generous to Jinx and completely honest about the bill.

Wondrous item, legacy item (requires attunement by Jinx)

Your Charges

The Luck Charges pool grows on its own at 6th, 10th and 15th level. You never have to update the sheet — the number just changes.

StateYour levelLuck ChargesBack at dawn
Dormantlevels 3–53all of them
Awakenedlevels 6–95all of them
Exaltedlevels 10–1471d6 + 1
Legendarylevel 15+91d8 + 1

At Dormant and Awakened every spent charge comes back. From 10th level it stops refilling completely: the pool is bigger, and a heavy day stays expensive into the next one.

Legacy Save DC

Where a feature makes something roll a saving throw, the DC is 8 + proficiency bonus + spellcasting ability modifier. It comes off your sheet, so it rises as you do.

What Unlocks When

Features arrive on their own. Below its level a feature is not on the item at all, so anything you can see on the sheet is something you can use. Where a later state improves an earlier feature, the old version disappears and the new one takes its place.

Dormant — levels 3–5 (Uncommon): Double or Nothing; Liar's Coin; Surely Magic Is Relevant.

Awakened — levels 6–9 (Rare): Push Your Luck; That's Not How That Spell Works.

Exalted — levels 10–14 (Very Rare): That's DEFINITELY Not How That Spell Works; All In; I Meant To Do That.

Legendary — level 15+ (Legendary): The Impossible Bet; Rewrite the Rules; The Coin Lands Sideways.

Advancing

Reaching the level makes the next state possible. What actually wakes the item is the moment named at the top of each state below — a choice, not an achievement, and never something you can win in a fight. You do not need to chase it. When it happens, you will know, and so will the item.

pages.name: Levels 3–5 — Dormant
pages.html:
Uncommon · levels 3–5 · 3 Luck Charges, all of them returning at dawn

Where it starts. This is the item as you first receive it. Everything below is yours from the moment you attune.

Everything from earlier states still works unless a feature here says it replaces one.

Double or Nothing

No action — 1 charge

After Jinx fails an attack roll, ability check or saving throw, he may expend 1 charge and roll 1d6. On a 1–2 the original roll stands. On a 3–6 he rerolls the d20 and adds 1d4. He must use the new result.

Liar's Coin

No action — 1× per short or long rest

Jinx learns minor illusion. Once per short or long rest, when making a Deception, Performance or Sleight of Hand check, he may treat a d20 result of 9 or lower as 10.

Surely Magic Is Relevant

No action — 1 charge

Jinx can expend 1 charge before making an ability check to use Intelligence in place of its normal ability. He must provide some remotely plausible magical explanation.

pages.name: Levels 6–9 — Awakened
pages.html:
Rare · levels 6–9 · 5 Luck Charges, all of them returning at dawn

What wakes it. Jinx has a genuine opportunity to escape serious danger and deliberately stays because something or someone matters more.

Everything from earlier states still works unless a feature here says it replaces one.

Push Your Luck

Push Your Luck. No action — no cost

Push Your Luck — The Bill. No action — 2d6 psychic

After Double or Nothing turns a failure into a success, Jinx may Push. Roll 1d6:

  • 1–3: the success remains, but Jinx takes 2d6 psychic damage;
  • 4–5: the success remains and the Luck Charge is refunded;
  • 6: the success becomes extraordinary — an attack becomes a critical hit, and an ability check or saving throw is treated as though the d20 rolled 20.

The psychic damage ignores resistance.

That's Not How That Spell Works

No action — 1× per long rest

Once per long rest when casting a spell, Jinx may choose one:

  • change acid, cold, fire, lightning or thunder damage into another type on that list;
  • double the spell's range, to a maximum of 300 feet;
  • remove its verbal component;
  • remove its somatic component.

pages.name: Levels 10–14 — Exalted
pages.html:
Very Rare · levels 10–14 · 7 Luck Charges, regaining 1d6 + 1 at dawn

What wakes it. Jinx knowingly takes a dangerous magical risk for something more important than proving that he can.

Everything from earlier states still works unless a feature here says it replaces one.

That's DEFINITELY Not How That Spell Works

No action — proficiency bonus× per long rest

That's Not How That Spell Works can now be used a number of times per long rest equal to Jinx's proficiency bonus, but only once per spell. It also gains:

  • Bend. If a spell affects a line, cone, cube or sphere, Jinx can exclude a number of creatures equal to his Intelligence modifier, minimum one.
  • Stretch. A spell with a duration of 1 minute or longer and no concentration requirement has its duration doubled, to a maximum of 24 hours.

This replaces the Awakened version.

All In

All In. No action — 2 charges

All In — The Bill. No action — 3d6 psychic

When Jinx uses Double or Nothing, he may spend 2 charges instead of 1. He immediately rerolls the d20 with advantage and adds 1d4. If both advantage dice would fail the original DC or AC, Jinx suffers 3d6 psychic damage and cannot use Double or Nothing again until the end of his next turn.

I Meant To Do That

No action — 1× per short or long rest

Once per short or long rest, after Jinx triggers a trap, activates an unknown magical effect or causes an unintended magical consequence, he may gain resistance to all damage caused by that initial triggering effect and advantage on its first saving throw. The accident still happens. Jinx is simply astonishingly good at surviving Jinx.

pages.name: Level 15+ — Legendary
pages.html:
Legendary · level 15+ · 9 Luck Charges, regaining 1d8 + 1 at dawn

What wakes it. Jinx reaches a moment where chance, magic and bravado could give him extraordinary personal power, and deliberately gambles it for somebody else.

Everything from earlier states still works unless a feature here says it replaces one.

The Impossible Bet

No action — 1× per long rest

Once per long rest, before rolling a d20, Jinx can announce an Impossible Bet, naming the specific action and intended outcome. Roll two d20s. Jinx chooses one; the other becomes a Debt Die. Before Jinx's next long rest the DM may replace one d20 Jinx rolls with the Debt Die, after Jinx rolls but before the outcome is determined. If the unused Debt Die was a natural 20, the DM cannot use it and the debt disappears. Jinx literally borrows luck from his future.

Rewrite the Rules

No action — 1× per long rest

Once per long rest, when Jinx casts a spell of 5th level or lower, he can apply two different That's Not How That Spell Works modifications to it.

The Coin Lands Sideways

No action — 1× per long rest

Once per long rest, when Jinx rolls a natural 1 or a natural 20, he can flip the result: 1 becomes 20, or 20 becomes 1. Why would he voluntarily turn a 20 into a 1? Because there will eventually be a reason.

pages.name: Playing It Well
pages.html:
Every tier of the Coin asks the same question in a louder voice: you have already succeeded, so are you going to push it again? The item is generous to Jinx and completely honest about the bill.

At the Table

  • Spend Double or Nothing on failed saves before failed attacks. A missed attack costs one attack. A failed save often costs the fight.
  • Push Your Luck is a second, separate decision. Half the time (1–3) it holds the success and hurts him, and the psychic damage ignores resistance, so nothing he owns reduces it.
  • All In replaces the one-charge spend. Two charges total, not three.
  • I Meant To Do That is insurance against being Jinx. Hold it for the trap he did not mean to set off rather than spending it on a fight.
  • The Impossible Bet is a genuine loan. Call it when the roll in front of him matters more than any roll he will make before his next long rest.

Questions That Come Up

Can Push Your Luck follow All In?
Yes. Push Your Luck triggers when Double or Nothing turns a failure into a success, and All In is a way of spending Double or Nothing.

When does a refunded charge come back?
Immediately, on a 4–5. He can spend it again the same turn.

Can That's Not How That Spell Works change damage to necrotic or radiant?
No. Acid, cold, fire, lightning and thunder only, and only into one another.

What happens if the DM never uses the Debt Die?
It expires at his next long rest, and so does the debt.

Why would he ever turn a natural 20 into a 1?
Because a critical success is not always the outcome he wants. That is the whole reason the feature is written both ways.

If Something Here Disagrees With the Item

The item on your sheet is the rules. This journal is generated from the same source, so the two should never differ — but if they do, the item wins and your DM should know.
